title: Allosteric inhibition rescues hydrocephalus caused by catalytically inactive Shp2 in mice
content:
by Neoklis Makrides, Emily Sun, Hilal Mir, Jen-Zen Chuang, Ziyuan Jiang, Yihua Wu, Carlos Serra, John Peregrin, Qian Wang, Wellington V. Cardoso, Ching-Hwa Sung, Neel H. Shah, Xin Zhang

SHP2, a protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) crucial in Ras-MAPK signaling, is associated with various human congenital diseases and cancers. Here, we show that the catalytically inactive Shp2C459S mutation results in communicating hydrocephalus, similar to the catalytically activating Shp2E76K and Mek1DD mutants. Unlike previous mutants, however, Shp2C459S/+ mutation uniquely affects ciliary development rather than neurogenesis, leading to structural abnormalities in cilia and impaired ciliary motility. Differential scanning fluorimetry suggested that SHP2C459S, SHP2E76K, and SHP2C459S/E76K mutations all induce an open SHP2 conformation, but only SHP2C459S leads to aberrant GAB1 phosphorylation in cells expressing wild-type SHP2. Consistent with this distinct signaling profile, brain ventricular tissues from Shp2C459S/+ mice exhibit elevated GAB1 and AKT phosphorylation despite normal ERK and STAT3 activities, implicating dysregulated PI3K–AKT signaling in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K markedly rescues ciliogenesis defects and alleviates hydrocephalus in mutant mice. Furthermore, the allosteric SHP2 inhibitor SHP099 increases the thermal stability of SHP2C459S protein, consistent with a shift toward a closed state, and ameliorates hydrocephalus in Shp2C459S/+ mice. These findings suggest that, in this engineered mouse model, Shp2-associated hydrocephalus is driven by conformational changes rather than altered catalytic activity. Our results underscore the therapeutic potential of conformation-specific allosteric inhibitors in targeting both catalytically active and inactive SHP2 mutants.
